entries.title: The whole article, at any level of detail
entries.body: Spideryarn lays a piece out as columns of increasing detail — a sentence on the argument, then its parts, its sections, and the original text beside them — and you move up and down the levels with the pointer, the arrow keys or a swipe. Summary mode writes any part or section in a sentence, briefly, or at length, and every row links back to the paragraphs it came from. Diagram mode draws the same structure as a picture.

entries.title: The words and ideas a piece assumes
entries.body: Glossary mode collects the terms an article uses as though you already knew them, keeping what a word means in this piece separate from general background. Terms are underlined in the text itself; point at one and its definition appears beside it, and you can step through every place the piece uses it. Ideas mode does the same for the propositions an article assumes, and marks the ones it never argues for.

entries.title: Search the article by words or by meaning
entries.body: Search finds an exact phrase in the piece at once, or you can describe what you are looking for and get the passages that answer it, best first, appearing as they arrive. Hits are highlighted in the text and drawn as coloured lanes down the edge of the article, so you can see where a search's answers cluster. Meaning searches are saved, and several can be shown at once in different colours.

entries.title: Ask about a passage, or the whole piece
entries.body: Select any sentence and a small box opens beside it. Ask a question — or nothing at all, and you get an explanation of what you need to bring to that passage — and the answer appears as it is written, anchored to the passage so you can find it again. Chat mode talks to the whole article, citing the paragraphs it draws on, and can search this piece, look into another article in your library, read a page from the web, or check the glossary.

entries.title: Add an article from a link or PDF
entries.body: Paste an address and the piece is fetched and prepared for reading, with its progress shown as it goes. A PDF is read a page at a time and every page checked against the file's own text; where a page cannot be checked, the article says so and links to the original scan. Each article keeps a page recording where it came from, how long it is and how it was read, and adding the same piece twice is recognised as one article.

entries.title: Your library, your account, your words
entries.body: You sign in with Google or an email address, and everything you add sits in a library you can sort, search and archive. The text you select and the questions you ask are kept out of error messages and logs, and an article is cleaned before it is shown so that a page cannot run code inside the app. A profile page holds a note on who you are and what you want from a piece, which the glossary, the summaries and chat answers can be written for.

entries.title: When something fails, it says so plainly
entries.body: Where a failure used to arrive as raw technical text, or as a spinner that never stopped, it comes as a plain sentence saying what happened and whether trying again would help. The retry button is hidden when a second attempt cannot come out differently, and an answer that stalls gives up and tells you.

entries.title: Hyperlinks in an article show a hover card
entries.body: Point at a hyperlink in the article, or move to it with the keyboard, and a small card appears telling you where it goes, so you can judge whether it is worth following before you leave the paragraph. Where the linked words are also a term in the article's glossary, you get one card carrying both, rather than two cards covering the same words.

entries.title: The app would not load; it does now
entries.body: For a period, every page of the app failed: nothing opened and no request came back. The part that reads PDFs was being started on every single request, and failing there. It is now started only when an article actually needs it, so the rest of the app comes up whatever happens.

entries.title: Your articles are visible only to you
entries.body: While signed in, you could be shown somebody else's library rather than your own, and could delete from it. Every page now checks that the article belongs to the account asking for it; an article you do not own is not found. The same check now covers uploaded PDFs and the list of articles being added.

entries.title: Delete an article from its own page
entries.body: An article's Metadata page now has a Delete control of its own, so you can remove a piece without going back to your library. It archives rather than erases, and Put back stays there for as long as you want it. The buttons across your library were also redrawn: many carried a stray outline and the wrong colours.

entries.title: Tabs are named after the article in them
entries.body: With several articles open, every tab used to read the same thing. A tab now shows the article's own title and the mode it is in, so you can tell them apart at a glance, and screen readers are told when it changes.

entries.title: Link previews say more about the destination
entries.body: Point at a link in an article and the card shows the whole address. If the link goes to something already in your library, the card adds its title, a short summary and how long it takes to read; a Wikipedia link adds that page's own description; a DOI or arXiv link is recognised as one.

entries.title: Force draws lines between similar passages
entries.body: In Diagram mode, the Force picture now joins passages that say similar things with dotted lines, worked out when you open that picture. Its reading-order lines run as one chain through the whole piece rather than breaking at each part, and links the article makes to itself are drawn too.

entries.title: A front page for people arriving signed out
entries.body: Somebody who opens Spideryarn without an account used to meet a sign-in form and nothing else. They now get a page saying what the app does, with pictures of the reading view, and the sign-in buttons on the page itself.

entries.title: The app goes quiet in a background tab
entries.body: When you switch to another tab, checks on articles being added and the times shown on screen stop until you come back, then catch up straight away. Scrolling with a Diagram picture open no longer re-runs its layout on every scroll. An article being added keeps going while you are away.

entries.title: Two things you could get stuck on
entries.body: A long list in the Ideas panel ran past the bottom with no way to reach the rest of it; the panel scrolls now, group headings stay in view, and a link to one idea opens it and marks its passage. Reloading the page that waits for an uploaded PDF used to land on a broken address; it reloads properly.

entries.title: Diagram mode adds Drift and Trail pictures
entries.body: Diagram mode has two new pictures of a whole article. Drift places every paragraph by what it is about, so you can see where the piece clusters and where it strays; Trail draws the paragraphs in the order they come, so you can see how it moves from one to the next. Labels, spacing and the reading-order line were all reworked after the pictures first appeared, so both read clearly at a glance.

entries.title: Your library opens on what you read last
entries.body: The library now sorts by when you last opened an article rather than when you added it, with ones you have never opened at the bottom. The box for adding articles shows only what you started in this tab; older imports sit behind an 'earlier' link that still flags any failures.

entries.title: Picking one saved search takes one click
entries.body: In Search, pressing a saved search marks that one and unmarks the rest, so moving between them takes a single press. The checkbox beside it still adds a search to the ones already marked, for the times you want several at once. Reaching the row with the keyboard now shows the same focus outline as the rest of the app.

entries.title: The home page says what this is, plainly
entries.body: The top of the signed-out home page has been rewritten. It makes the same claims as before, stated directly in the app's own voice rather than through a personal quote.

entries.title: The dictation microphone shows what it is doing
entries.body: On your profile page, the microphone button shows an opening step before it starts listening, with a live meter of the sound it picks up, so you can tell it is working. Errors that used to switch it off in silence now say what went wrong, and speech is no longer lost when dictation ends on its own.

entries.title: Your profile shows one name per AI
entries.body: The profile page lists the AI work done on your articles. The same AI could be listed under two different names depending on how it had been asked, which made it look as though more were in use than there were. Each one now appears once, under a single name.

entries.title: Home page pictures are no longer stretched
entries.body: The screenshot on the signed-out home page was being drawn taller than it should be, so it looked warped. Pictures outside the article text keep their proper shape again.

entries.title: The signed-out home page shows real screenshots
entries.body: The page you see before signing in now shows real screenshots of four things the app does: the glossary and its link cards, search by meaning, a paragraph diagram, and zooming in and out of a piece, each with a few lines about it. The pictures are sharper than the ones they replace.

entries.title: Signing in with Google no longer leaves the app
entries.body: Choosing Continue with Google could send you away from Spideryarn to a page of raw error text when Google sign-in was not switched on. The button now checks first: if it is unavailable, you stay on the sign-in screen, with the email form and a message telling you why.

entries.title: Choose the colour of a saved search
entries.body: Each saved search in Search mode has a colour that marks its hits in the text. You can now pick that colour yourself, from a grid of sixteen hues arranged in hue order, or set it back to the automatic one. Searches you saved before keep the colour they had.

entries.title: Diagram drops the pictures that repeated others
entries.body: Four picture types that drew the same shapes as others have been removed, and Diagram opens on Tree by default, the one picture that needs no work from the AI. Each remaining choice has a hover card saying what that picture shows and what it costs. Arrow keys no longer scroll the article while you move between nodes.

entries.title: Scrolling a long article costs less work
entries.body: Scrolling the reading view caused a burst of processor use, because the strip showing where you are and the columns beside the text were redrawn dozens of times a second. Both are redrawn far less often, so a long piece scrolls with less work behind it.

entries.title: Dictation names the microphone it is using
entries.body: When a dictation produced no words, there was no way to tell that the microphone the browser had chosen was recording silence. The microphone is now named, you can pick a different one, and a recording that transcribed nothing is kept as a file you can download. The button on your profile page says dictation is unreliable.

entries.title: Dictation recordings that captured nothing
entries.body: The recorder could fail before it produced any sound, without saying so, leaving dictation with nothing to transcribe. It falls back to other recording settings when one fails, and audio from a failed attempt can no longer end up at the front of the next recording.

entries.title: Diagram tooltips, labels and step buttons
entries.body: A picture-type tooltip could land to the side and cover its neighbours; it stays under the chip. Two labels in one picture could read as the same word. The step buttons looked disabled, named the wrong unit and could send you to the wrong paragraph. While a picture is still loading, you see a Tree rather than nothing.

entries.title: Keep reading when the connection drops
entries.body: An article you have already opened — its text, its levels of detail, its glossary, summaries, ideas and chat — is now kept on your own device, so if the network fails you carry on reading, with a notice telling you that is what you are seeing. Lists you can edit, such as chat and comments, are left out once you have written to them, so nothing you saved is replaced by an older copy.

entries.title: The reading view works on a phone
entries.body: On a narrow screen the article no longer runs off the side of the window with every line cut mid-word: the column fits the window, the panel beside the article opens full screen, and all of the mode buttons can be reached and pressed. On a short screen the controls bar gets out of the way as you scroll down.

entries.title: Rename an article from the article itself
entries.body: The pencil for renaming an article now sits at the top of the article and on its Metadata page, not only in your library, so you can correct a title at the moment you notice it is wrong.

entries.title: Your library page opens faster
entries.body: Listing your articles was fetching the whole original document behind each one, for a page that only shows titles, counts and a blurb. It now asks for what it shows, and opens faster.

entries.title: The document an article came from is kept
entries.body: When you add an article, the document it was taken from is kept and tied to that version of it. If we already hold a copy, it is read back and checked before anything relies on it, and if it does not match, the app stops and says so rather than writing over what is there.

entries.title: The You page is now called Profile
entries.body: The page with your reading profile, and its link from your library, are labelled Profile rather than You. The browser tab says Profile too, which makes it easier to pick out when you have several open.

entries.title: Adding an article fails more quietly
entries.body: When adding an article went wrong, the page could print the raw query it had tried, in red, under the Add box; it no longer does. Dropping a PDF now starts the upload straight away, and a second file dropped while one is still going is refused rather than tangling with it.

entries.title: Articles publish only once their levels are built
entries.body: A version of an article could be published while the work that builds the outline you zoom in and out of had failed or was still running, so the article could appear with a broken set of levels. It now waits until that work has finished properly.

entries.title: Column buttons say what each column holds
entries.body: The buttons that show and hide the columns beside the article are labelled Arg and Para, instead of L0 and a number that changed from one article to the next. Point at a button and a short line tells you what that column contains. A tooltip that read "the the" has been corrected.

entries.title: Profile page names the AI behind each job
entries.body: The table on your profile page that lists which AI handles each part of an article now shows both the AI's name and how the app reaches it. Behind that, every part of building an article goes through one AI service rather than a mix of them.

entries.title: Review: say what you took, and find out
entries.body: There is a new Review tab beside the article. You write what you took from the piece, in your own words, and the answer points out where your account and the article part company. You choose the stance it answers in — Balanced, Respond, Socratic or Signposts — and there is nothing to say until you have done the reading, which is the point of it.

entries.title: Share an article with someone without an account
entries.body: You can mark one of your own articles as shared and send its address to someone who has never signed in, and they can read it. They see the article itself, not the parts that belong to your account: your comments and your conversations are not part of what they get. If an address is wrong or the article is not shared, they are told that rather than being dropped on the front page.

entries.title: Comments and bookmarks without asking the AI
entries.body: Selecting a passage opens a box where you can write a comment or simply mark the place, and asking the AI is a separate tick-box rather than something that happens whether you wanted it or not. Saved comments can be edited afterwards, and one you did ask about reopens its conversation. The Questions panel is now called Comments.

entries.title: Preview cards work on phones and tablets
entries.body: On a touchscreen, tapping the strip that shows where you are in the article opens a preview of that section, and tapping the same place again jumps to it. A glossary term in the text works the same way, where before a tap did nothing at all. The article also scrolls only up and down under a finger.

entries.title: Your library and article panels load faster
entries.body: Listing a small library took over half a second and now takes about three milliseconds, and the Glossary, Summary and Ideas panels no longer wait while the article is fetched again for work already done. When one of those lists cannot be fetched, you are told, rather than shown an empty one.

entries.title: Four smaller changes across the app
entries.body: Dictation checks its own recording a second time against the article's glossary, so terms from the piece come out right, and it works in Firefox. Chat can look at the article's own links rather than guess where they lead. In the Summary panel, the badge under a part opens that part's sections alone, and paragraphs sit closer together.

entries.title: Freezes, blank pages and overwritten chats
entries.body: The library page could lock up the moment you typed in the Add or search box; it does not now. When a page went wrong while being drawn it went blank with nothing to say why, and now shows a short message. A conversation you just started or deleted can no longer be replaced by a refresh of the list.

entries.title: Missing text recovered, hidden formula code removed
entries.body: Text inside collapsed or expandable sections was dropped when an article was added — on one page, roughly a quarter of it — and it comes through now. On pages with mathematics, the source behind each formula was ending up in the text itself, where copying, reading aloud and search picked it up; it is taken out now.

entries.title: Footnotes and sidenotes come through with the article
entries.body: When you add an article that uses footnotes, endnotes or margin notes — Wikipedia and Substack pieces among them — the note text arrives with it and sits with the passage it belongs to, instead of showing up as an empty marker. Notes that already worked keep their links back to the text, and a highlight or comment you attached to one of those passages stays where you put it.

entries.title: Dictation knows the words in the article
entries.body: When you dictate into a box beside an article — a comment, a question in Chat, what you are reading it for — the transcription draws on that article's glossary, the names it uses, and the vocabulary from your profile. Hard terms and proper nouns come out right more often.

entries.title: Diagram says why placing passages failed
entries.body: In Diagram, the Force, Drift and Trail views place passages by meaning. When that failed they all showed the same message asking you to try again, whatever had gone wrong. Each failure now says which it is: not set up, the service unreachable, or too many requests at once.

entries.title: Access & Sharing shows the real state
entries.body: The Access & Sharing card, where you choose who can see an article, could not tell a private article from one it had failed to check, so it always said it could not check. It reads the article's own settings instead, and the date you made it public stays visible after a reload.

entries.title: Renaming a chat conversation sticks
entries.body: If you renamed a conversation in Chat and the request was slow, opening it and editing your first question could bring the old name back. The new name is kept from the moment you ask for it. Loading and deleting conversations were reworked the same way, so a slow request cannot leave the wrong conversation on screen.

entries.title: Clearer wording on a shared article
entries.body: On an article someone has shared with you, the comments drawer is headed Comments rather than Your comments. A warning that a mode is not available for this article names the mode you picked, and visitors who are already signed in are no longer asked to create a free account.

entries.title: Switching accounts clears the article on screen
entries.body: If you signed out and someone else signed in on the same browser, the article already open could stay on screen, a private one included, with the controls only its owner should see. The page now checks who is reading rather than only whether anyone is signed in, so it clears when the account changes. Pointing at a link in the article also no longer sends requests when nobody is signed in.

entries.title: Links out no longer reveal where you were
entries.body: When you follow a link out of an article, the site you land on is no longer told which page you came from. That holds on every page of the app, not only while you are reading.

entries.title: Shared articles say what they actually have
entries.body: On an article shared with you, the page could say a glossary or a set of ideas was missing when it had only failed to check, and could show wording written for the owner. It now says when it does not know, and the link to the original file appears only for the owner.

entries.title: Access and Sharing says what really happened
entries.body: If turning sharing on or off failed, the Access & Sharing card could tell you the article was unchanged when the change had already been saved, or say only you can read it when it had not managed to check. It now reports what it could not confirm, and stays on screen.

entries.title: Cancelling a chat message just after sending works
entries.body: Stopping a message, a retry or an edit in Chat in the moment after you sent it could report that it had stopped while the answer carried on. In one case it brought back a conversation you had deleted. Both are fixed.

entries.title: A background check no longer wipes the list
entries.body: In Ideas, Summary and on the tweet-thread page, a list you were already reading could be replaced by an error when the app quietly rechecked it and that check failed. The list now stays. When something does fail, the message says what went wrong rather than blaming the connection, and that reloading tries again.

entries.title: Adding a PDF recovers from an interruption
entries.body: If adding a PDF was interrupted part-way, the half-written result was kept and every later attempt at that article failed, with nothing on screen to say why and no way to clear it. A part-written result is now discarded and those pages are read again.

entries.title: Footnotes are part of the reading view
entries.body: Footnote and citation markers are now recognised: point at one and the note appears in a card without losing your place, and following a note remembers which passage you came from. Notes get their own Footnotes entry in the strip beside the article, and are kept out of the piece's argument — not summarised, not drawn as paragraphs, and no longer counted in the reading-time estimate, which fell from 73 minutes to 55 on one heavily annotated article. Search and Chat still find them.

entries.title: A new Outline mode shows the whole piece
entries.body: Outline sits alongside the other modes and shows the whole document as a nested list that never scrolls: it opens out around wherever you are and folds up everywhere else. It is there for the people you share an article with as well, who can also read that article's Glossary, Ideas and Summary panels and see its terms marked in the text.

entries.title: Figures, tables and code can be enlarged
entries.body: Pictures and diagrams sit on a light sheet, so tables and equations drawn in near-black ink read as they should rather than dark on dark. Bigger images, tables and code blocks open at close to full screen, with the links inside them still working.

entries.title: The strip beside the article is slimmer
entries.body: The navigation strip down the side of the article is half its old width, leaving more room for the text. Point at it and the card lists the sections it covers and where you are among them, instead of empty bullets — and the cards appear at all again, after a recent change had stopped them.

entries.title: Spideryarn can be added to your home screen
entries.body: Adding the app to a home screen now works, and iOS offers the prompt once; installed, it has no browser bars around it. On a phone both bars slide away together as you read and the controls at the foot are larger. A note card no longer pushes the page sideways, and the view-only notice no longer overlaps the logo.

entries.title: Cancelled chat answers stay cancelled
entries.body: Stopping an answer while it was being written did not always reach the server, so a conversation you had discarded came back on the next reload. Renaming or deleting one just after starting it could be lost, or could overwrite a title you had typed. Both now wait until the conversation exists, then apply.

entries.title: When something is refused, you are told why
entries.body: Rebuilding an article from your library looked as though it had worked even when the request was turned down. And when a glossary, a set of ideas, a summary or a thread could not be started, the reason was replaced a moment later by a general message. Both show what actually came back, and clear once a run starts.

entries.title: Re-running an article keeps what is attached
entries.body: Re-processing an article could detach comments, saved searches and contents entries pinned to its passages, and “Find more terms” could reset the glossary and break links to a term. It stops instead, when it cannot see what was there before. A page with no readable text is refused as you add it, rather than landing in your library empty.

entries.title: Shared article links preview with their title
entries.body: When you share a link to a public article, the preview card in a chat app or on social media now carries that article's own title and a short description of it. Until now every such link previewed as the bare word Spideryarn, whichever piece it pointed at, so nobody could tell one from another.

entries.title: Contents is now called Hierarchy
entries.body: The mode that shows the article at its levels of detail is labelled Hierarchy in the bar at the bottom, and named that way in the page's address too. Links you saved under the old name still open it.

entries.title: Articles are ready to read sooner
entries.body: Adding an article no longer waits for the leftmost, coarsest column of Hierarchy to be built first: about ten seconds off a wait of roughly four minutes, measured once on a real article. If you open the piece before that column exists, it is built while you read and drops in when it is ready.

entries.title: Comments and highlights survive a new footnote
entries.body: If a source added or removed a footnote, every passage below it looked like new text the next time we took a fresh copy of the article, and whatever you had attached to those passages — comments, highlights, where you had got to — came loose. The words had not changed, so they now stay put.

entries.title: The leftmost Hierarchy column keeps up
entries.body: After an article's levels of detail were rebuilt, the leftmost column in Hierarchy could go on showing a single line about the whole piece where there should be a sentence for each section. It now notices when what it was built from has changed, and is built again.

entries.title: A malformed article address sends you to your library
entries.body: An address the app can never answer — one with capital letters in it, say — used to try to open the article and then show you an error. It takes you to your library instead.

entries.title: Sketch draws the shape of an article's argument
entries.body: Diagram has a new picture, Sketch: the AI draws the shape of the piece's reasoning — what supports what, where the asides hang off — as a drawing you can click into. Each part opens a closer view, and every closer view is listed as a chip along the bar, so you can reach all of them whether or not the drawing links to them. It works with a keyboard and a screen reader.

entries.title: Articles you add reach your library
entries.body: Adding an article on the site could stop part-way, or finish and never show up in your library. The parts that take longest — working out the article's levels of detail, and writing its summaries — now have room to finish, the work carries on rather than starting over, and an article that finishes is put in your library. A piece with many figures no longer keeps fetching them from the original site after it has stopped collecting.

entries.title: Diagram opens with Force, and Tree has gone
entries.body: The Tree picture has been taken out, and Diagram opens on Force. Trail and Drift show a wait, or the reason they could not be drawn, rather than another picture's shape. Their up and down buttons no longer send you back to the top of the section, and the browser's Back button no longer pulls you forward again.

entries.title: Summaries follow your profile, not a separate box
entries.body: The Summary panel no longer asks separately what you are reading the piece for. That question already sits on your profile, as why you are reading this one, and it reaches the longer summaries through the Use your profile box. Unticking that box just before asking for the summaries again now takes effect.

entries.title: Outline mode's rows are readable and indented
entries.body: Outline mode's text was painted almost the same shade as the panel behind it, and the row you were reading was not marked at all. The rows read clearly now, each row's number sits beside its title instead of pushing it onto a second line, and nested rows are indented so you can see what sits under what.

entries.title: Adding an article twice no longer overwrites it
entries.body: On the site, adding a piece you had already added could replace the one you had, taking its comments, chat threads, saved searches and glossary lookups with it. The app now checks properly whether you already have that article, so nothing of yours is replaced.

entries.title: The profile badge beside AI answers opens
entries.body: The badge beside summaries, glossary entries, ideas and chat answers carried a link that never opened anything. Clicking it opens a panel showing the background and the purpose the answer was written for, with links to edit either. The button is there even when you have not written a profile yet.

entries.title: Tab titles settle and shared links show cards
entries.body: The browser tab's title could change to something else a moment after a page opened, and older article addresses did not always land where they should. Both are fixed. A shared article link pasted into a chat or a social site shows a card for the piece, while the pages stay out of search results.

entries.title: Adding a PDF article works
entries.body: Adding an article from a PDF failed every time on the live site: the import stopped moments after it started and no article appeared. The missing piece has been supplied, and a PDF goes through like any other article.

entries.title: Sketch diagrams open at full window width
entries.body: The Sketch picture has an Enlarge button that draws it across the whole window, in place of the zoom toggle that only made things bigger inside the narrow panel beside the article. Region names are clickable as well, so you can open the closer-in picture of a section by clicking its name.

entries.title: Diagram links fade with distance from you
entries.body: In the Trail and Force pictures, the two connections either side of where you are reading are drawn at full strength, and each further step along the chain fades towards the ordinary weight. It is easier to see where in the chain you are sitting. Both pictures are behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: The Diagram panel shows when it is working
entries.body: While a picture is being drawn, the panel says so instead of sitting unchanged until it arrives, including when the drawing was started from somewhere else. Pointing at Sketch's Back, scene and Enlarge controls brings up a short card saying what each one does, on a touchscreen as well as with a mouse.

entries.title: A picture stays put when a refresh fails
entries.body: When a check for a newer version of a picture failed, the picture you already had was cleared and you were left with nothing. It stays on screen instead. Where something does fail to load, there is a button to try again rather than a dead end.

entries.title: Diagram controls can be used from the keyboard
entries.body: In Diagram mode, the word chips in the lane legend and the scene buttons in Sketch can be reached with the keyboard and moved between with the arrow keys. Before, they answered only to a mouse.

entries.title: Diagram explanations match what the diagrams do
entries.body: Several of the hover explanations in Diagram described behaviour the diagrams did not have; they have been corrected. Switching between Force, Drift and Trail no longer sends a request the app had already made for the same article, and when a build fails the message refers to the run you are watching rather than an earlier one.

entries.title: Articles no longer lose their table of contents
entries.body: When the app works out an article's levels of detail, a boundary in slightly the wrong place could stop the whole thing, leaving no table of contents to move through; small slips are now corrected instead. Where a heading cannot be confirmed as the author's own, it loses that mark but keeps its place and wording.

entries.title: PDFs no longer fail to be added
entries.body: Adding a PDF could fail before it started, and papers with a stamp printed sideways down the margin were turned away as badly transcribed. Both are fixed: the sideways stamp is recognised for what it is, and a page the text check is unhappy about no longer stops the article going through.

entries.title: Labels in Diagram open the closer picture
entries.body: In Diagram mode, pressing the name of a labelled area in the zoomed-out picture takes you to the closer picture of that part, including on diagrams drawn before this worked. The name of the picture you are looking at is also shown in full rather than cut off.

entries.title: Publishing warns about a personalised diagram
entries.body: When you make an article public, the confirmation lists what of your own is going public with it. A diagram you had personalised was missing from that list, so you could be told nothing personal would be shared when it would. It is on the list.

entries.title: A link you cannot open gives nothing away
entries.body: Follow a link to an article that has not been shared with you and the browser tab now says so, rather than keeping the title of the page you were looking at before. That page is meant to reveal nothing, including whether the article exists.

entries.title: Quotes mode keeps the lines worth keeping
entries.body: A new Quotes mode picks out the memorable lines of a piece. Every suggestion is checked word for word against the article itself, and any that does not match is dropped with a note saying so, so what you read is the author's own text rather than a paraphrase of it. Surviving quotes are ranked by how important and how striking they are, drawn as bars beside each one.

entries.title: Talk to an article out loud
entries.body: Press Live in a conversation you already have open and you can speak to the article instead of typing. What you say and what comes back is kept in that same conversation, with pointers to the passages it drew on, and an interruption is marked where it happened. Press Send and you carry on by typing where you left off. A session closes itself after a stretch of quiet.

entries.title: Timeline lays out when things happened
entries.body: Timeline, between Ideas and Search on the mode bar, gathers the events an article describes and the dates it gives them. Each date is checked against the passage it came from; vague wording and dates that did not hold up are listed apart, and every row links back to the text. It appears on articles in your own library.

entries.title: Summary mode always has something to show
entries.body: Summary gives the one-sentence description of each part of a piece, at every level of detail. The longer versions that had to be written first are gone, so the panel is never empty or waiting, including on an article someone shared with you. The count of parts on an article opens and closes the list when you press it.

entries.title: Every article says where it came from
entries.body: At the top of an article, and on its Metadata page, you can see its origin: a link to the page it was taken from, a mark saying it was uploaded with a link to view the original, or a line saying no source was recorded. A shared article carries the link too, unless the address looks private.

entries.title: Sketch drawings show what opens up
entries.body: In Diagram mode, the parts of a sketch that open a drawing of their own stand out from the rest, and pointing at one previews what is inside before you press; going in and coming back are animated. Switching from a sketch to another Diagram view could leave the panel blank, and no longer does.

entries.title: Adding an article waits for less
entries.body: Only one article anywhere could be prepared at a time, so yours could sit behind somebody else's; up to three run at once. Long PDFs are read several pages at a time rather than one part after another, so a paper of many pages is far less likely to run out of time before it finishes.

entries.title: Articles that used to fail now finish
entries.body: Adding an article could stop with an error when one paragraph could not be labelled, or when its contents list came back cut short; it finishes now, leaving the odd paragraph unlabelled. A contents list could show a heading with the next paragraph's words, and a PDF word broken across a page could come back run together. Both fixed.

entries.title: Plain mode shows the article on its own
entries.body: Plain is now the view you start in: the article and nothing else, with no panel or extra columns beside it. Every mode has an X that closes it back to Plain, and on a phone the mode bar and the controls stay reachable while a panel is open — opening the keyboard in Search used to scroll both off the screen. The top bar also links to the original web page or uploaded PDF.

entries.title: Chat answers come back as lists and headings
entries.body: When you ask about a passage, the answer is laid out the way it was written — bullet lists, headings, quotations and code, rather than one run-on paragraph. Emphasis, links and the chips that point back to the passage a claim came from are drawn properly in Chat and in Summary entries.

entries.title: A narrow gutter beside each paragraph
entries.body: Each paragraph has a slim strip beside it carrying two small icons: one copies a link straight to that passage, and one marks a paragraph that has a comment on it. It replaces the row of grey text that used to sit there, and a stray gap above every paragraph is gone.

entries.title: A Referee panel and an experimental switch
entries.body: Referee appears in the mode bar for articles you own. Its Criteria, Claims, Mirror and Candidates views are placeholders — nothing is analysed there yet — and it says plainly that the article's text was sent to an AI service when it was added. Your profile page also has an Experimental features switch, with nothing behind it yet.

entries.title: Adding an article says where its text goes
entries.body: The page where you add an article tells you, before it starts, that the article's text is sent to an AI service to be processed. The privacy policy has the fuller account.

entries.title: Stepping through the article works everywhere
entries.body: Up and down step through the article and left and right change the level of detail, even when a chip or the mode bar has focus; those buttons used to swallow the keys. In Diagram, the step arrows move a paragraph at a time rather than skipping several, and the marker follows where you are in the text.

entries.title: Adding and refreshing an article fails less often
entries.body: When the levels of detail did not line up neatly with the article's own sections, adding it could fail outright; the app works the structure out from what it has instead. And retrying a failed refresh rebuilds the whole piece, rather than leaving the old text in place under a row of ticks.

entries.title: Boxed asides and captions look right
entries.body: Inside a boxed aside, the mark that signals the box no longer lands on quotations, code or captions within it, and a heading inside one keeps its place in the levels of detail. Captions picked out from the article are set narrower, smaller and fainter than the prose, as figure captions already were.

entries.title: A Quiz that asks you about the article
entries.body: The article can now put questions to you about what you have just read, and mark the answers you give. If the article is rebuilt after you have answered, the questions you had are kept and shown as out of date, rather than disappearing, so you can ask for a fresh set when you want one.

entries.title: Referee mode has a Criteria panel
entries.body: Referee mode can now judge a piece against criteria you set, passage by passage. Each passage is shaded by how well it meets the criterion, so the places that satisfy it and the places that fall short are visible without reading the whole piece twice.

entries.title: New articles get a short code in their address
entries.body: The address of a new article now ends in a short code, in place of the number that used to be tacked on when the name was already taken. Because the code is chosen when the article is created, the Add page now shows the address with that ending left off instead of promising one it cannot know.

entries.title: Retry only runs on an article that failed
entries.body: Retry used to run again even on an article that had already finished, repeating work you had already paid for. It now works only on an article that failed or was cancelled. A failure at the end of adding an article also used to leave it showing "running" until it timed out; it now reports the failure.

entries.title: Adding by link says what has already happened
entries.body: When you add an article straight from a bookmarklet or a share sheet, there is no moment to stop it first, so the page now tells you plainly that the article's text has been sent to the AI service. The Add box in your library still warns you beforehand, where you can still change your mind.

entries.title: Referee mode stops inventing neutral verdicts
entries.body: In Referee mode's Criteria panel, a passage the AI had not actually weighed up was shown as counting neither for nor against, which looked identical to a real neutral judgement. Those results are now left out of the list and counted separately, so what you see is what was judged.

entries.title: Referee mode gains three panels
entries.body: Referee mode, for a paper you have been asked to review, has three more panels. Claims sets out what the paper asserts and where, and says when it has hit a limit rather than leaving a short list looking complete. Mirror reads your own comments back and remarks on their tone, coverage and placement. Candidates helps you build a shortlist of reviewers, with citations. A banner above them all reports whether the document carries instructions hidden in it for the AI.

entries.title: Download everything an article holds
entries.body: On an article you added, its details page has an Export button that downloads a zip of what we hold for it: the text with its byline, source and date, everything the app built from it, your comments, conversations, searches and referee work, with a readable index page explaining each file and what has been left out. The original document, its images and earlier versions are not included, and a very large bundle is refused rather than sent.

entries.title: Place a passage on your own criteria
entries.body: In Referee mode you can attach a passage to one of your criteria and mark where it sits, in that criterion's own words. Where the pairing is clear, your placement sits beside the model's; ambiguous ones and ones the model missed are listed separately. A criterion with no match says so as a fact about the search, not the paper.

entries.title: Review mode is now called Remember
entries.body: Review mode has been renamed Remember, which says what it is for rather than how it works; conversations you already had are still there. Its Quiz half lets you move between questions, see them all at once, reveal a reference answer when you want it, dictate your answer, and jump to the passage a question came from.

entries.title: Import progress keeps going as you move around
entries.body: Adding an article carries on while you visit other signed-in pages, so progress no longer stops because you looked at your profile. Its card shows how long the current step has been running, warns when a step is taking longer than usual or when the connection has stopped making progress, and says that a tab has to stay open.

entries.title: A Feedback button for reporting a problem
entries.body: When something goes wrong, there is a Feedback button on every signed-in page. It asks what you did, what you expected and what happened instead, takes an optional screenshot, and only sends diagnostics if you agree to it. A part-written report survives closing the dialog.

entries.title: Imports that stalled pick themselves up
entries.body: An import that stopped part-way is picked up again when you open your library, instead of sitting there frozen. Two people adding the same document at once no longer costs one of them their import, a long PDF that was retried resumes rather than starting over, and an older copy cannot overwrite a newer one.

entries.title: Half-finished answers are no longer marked complete
entries.body: When the AI stopped part-way, Quiz could tick the answer as marked and Explain and Search kept the partial text as though finished; all three report the failure. Notes and the counts beside them load again, a comment answer can be retried without reloading, comment edit errors are shown, and Referee's panel can no longer be pushed out of reach.

entries.title: Referee mode explains itself, and asks first
entries.body: Referee mode now carries short explanations on its controls and a card describing how the mode works, so you can look around without guessing what each part does. Its Candidates view no longer sends anything the moment you open it: looking for related work sits behind one button that names the AI service and the search engine before either sees your manuscript. Referee mode is under the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: Referee mode's opening notices fold away
entries.body: The two notices above Referee mode's controls — the one about your manuscript going to a third-party AI service, and the result of the check for hidden instructions in the text — start closed, so the page opens on the work rather than on prose you have already read. The hidden-instruction notice opens itself when it found something.

entries.title: Adding an article again no longer stalls
entries.body: When you added an article whose page had already been fetched and kept, the app tried to store it a second time, and a request could then wait out a minute-long timeout before anything happened. Large files such as PDFs suffered most. It now checks first and skips the upload.

entries.title: Referee marks now agree with the panel
entries.body: In Referee mode's Criteria view, a passage the panel called evidence against a criterion could be underlined in the article as evidence for it. Marks and panel swatches now share one scale across the mode, each carrying a sign, with a legend; the per-criterion colour choice is gone. Pressing a result also rings the exact phrase.

entries.title: Modes build themselves when you press them
entries.body: Press Glossary, Ideas, Quotes or Timeline on an article that does not have one yet and it starts building, instead of waiting for you to press a second button. The Sketch chip inside Diagram does the same. Arriving through a link, a bookmark or the Back button never starts anything on its own.

entries.title: A second request waits its turn
entries.body: Asking for Ideas while the Glossary was still building — or adding an article again mid-import — used to be turned away with a message saying the app was busy with this article. The second request is queued behind the first and runs when it can. Several ways an article could get stuck, blocking everything behind it, were fixed at the same time.

entries.title: A privacy page, and a simpler Feedback box
entries.body: There is a privacy page you can read before signing in: what we keep, who else handles it, and what you can ask for. It also says what a bug report carries, including the address of the page you were on. The Feedback box is a single box you write in, with a Problem or Suggestion choice and dictation.

entries.title: See what a shared link gives away
entries.body: Sharing an article now lists exactly what someone with the link can read, what stays private, and what would be published if you built it later. Your library also marks a shared article with a Shared badge, so you can tell at a glance which of your articles anyone with the link can open.

entries.title: Your article no longer opens as a stranger's
entries.body: If your browser could not reconfirm that you were signed in, your own article opened as though a stranger were reading it, with no way to sign in again. You now get a page saying your sign-in could not be confirmed, offering to sign you in again or carry on signed out — on every page of a shared article.

entries.title: Buttons that did nothing, or said too much
entries.body: Reading a shared article without an account, you saw a chat button beside every paragraph that did nothing when pressed; it is gone. Referee's opening button no longer claims what a search will cost, its wording matches the colours you actually see, and it tells a visitor plainly that Referee is for whoever added the article.

entries.title: The mode buttons stay on the screen
entries.body: In a window that was not wide enough, the last mode buttons ran off the edge where they could not be pressed. The row measures itself and hides labels as needed, and scrolls if even that is not enough. The duplicate link to the original article has gone from the controls; the mark beside the title still opens it.

entries.title: Panels no longer show an out-of-date version
entries.body: Opening Glossary, Ideas, Quotes, Timeline, Quiz or another panel while the app was still building something for that article could leave an older version on screen that never refreshed. Offline, Timeline, Quiz and a couple of others were not being kept at all, and answering one quiz question could lose the rest. Both are fixed.

entries.title: You can buy more article slots
entries.body: Adding an article takes one of your slots, and the slot comes back if the article is refused, cancelled or never finishes. Your profile page shows your plan, how much of your allowance you have used, and buttons to upgrade or manage your billing. When adding an article is refused because you are out of allowance, the message links straight there.

entries.title: Text in the panels is bigger
entries.body: The panels beside the article set some text as small as nine pixels, against seventeen for the article next to it. Every size in them has gone up, along with the cards that appear over the article, the comment and chat boxes, and your profile page. The article text itself is unchanged.

entries.title: The modes write in plainer language
entries.body: Hierarchy, Summary, Glossary, Ideas, Quotes, Timeline, Chat, Remember and its quiz ask the AI for ordinary language, while keeping the article's own words for the things it names. Diagrams drawn before this change are marked out of date, so one is drawn afresh the next time you open it.

entries.title: A private article's sharing card said too much
entries.body: The Access and Sharing card described what a shared link shows, in the present tense, even when the article was private and no link had been shared. It now lists what a link carries only where that is true, and the sentence that got it wrong is gone.

entries.title: Quizzes no longer fail on good questions
entries.body: Building a quiz could fail even when the questions it had were fine, leaving you with no quiz until you noticed and tried again. It stops only when the questions do not cover both the easy and the hard end, and the message you see if that happens is written in plain words.

entries.title: Diagram mode has a new Illustrated view
entries.body: Diagram mode has a new Illustrated view: a picture drawn for the article, with a list beside it of the moments it shows. Press one and the article moves to the passage it came from. Anything drawn has to be tied to a line the article actually says. A freshly drawn picture was reported as out of date the moment it appeared; it is not. Illustrated needs Experimental features turned on, along with the rest of Diagram mode.

entries.title: Some modes sit behind Experimental features
entries.body: Quotes, Timeline, Referee, Diagram and Remember are less finished than the rest, so they appear in the bar at the bottom only when Experimental features is turned on. Plain, Hierarchy, Outline, Summary, Glossary, Ideas, Search and Chat are there for everyone, signed in or not. A button at the end of the bar turns Experimental features on and off without leaving the article, and a link straight to one of the other modes still opens it. The switch on your profile page shows the right state more reliably.

entries.title: Raising the bar hides what falls below it
entries.body: In Glossary, Quotes and Search, the control that sets how much you want to see hides everything below the line instead of pushing it into a second group further down, and each says how many items are hidden. All three work the same way, and a term or quote you had picked can no longer stay selected after it disappears.

entries.title: An article's details page is reorganised
entries.body: The page showing an article's details leads with what matters to a reader, with identifiers and preparation details folded into a Technical details section that starts closed. A contents list in the margin follows you down the page. Several of its figures and its explanation of PDF quality were wrong and are corrected.

entries.title: Plain mode centres the article on the page
entries.body: In Plain mode, and anywhere else the article is the only column, the text sits in the middle of the window rather than against the left edge with a wide empty space to the right.

entries.title: Your library puts search above the list
entries.body: The search box sits directly above the articles it filters, and the box for adding an article takes about a fifth of a laptop screen where it took a third, so your articles start higher up the page, especially on a phone. When you are offline, the library shows only the articles you can still open.

entries.title: You are told when something has finished
entries.body: When the app makes something for an article, a glossary or a summary or a picture, you are told when it has finished, instead of showing nothing for ever. Start again in the Glossary panel had stopped working for everyone; it works again. When something does go wrong, the message explains it in plain words rather than technical detail.

entries.title: Plan prices include tax
entries.body: The price shown for a plan is the price charged: tax is included in it rather than added on top at payment. The plan descriptions on your profile page no longer repeat how many articles a month you get.

entries.title: Your library appears while it refreshes
entries.body: Your library draws straight away from a saved copy of the last time you looked, while the current list loads behind it, instead of holding you on a loading message. The app also loads its heavier parts only when a page needs them, so a first request spends just under a second less getting ready. And if one person signed out while the list was loading and another signed straight in, the page could show the first reader's articles; it cannot now.

entries.title: Pricing shows the plan you are on
entries.body: When you are signed in, the pricing page names your current plan, and the date it ends if you have cancelled. It also explains that the free articles are a lifetime allowance rather than a monthly one, and that cancelling does not reset them. Switching accounts no longer leaves the previous reader's plan on screen.

entries.title: Footer links, and a clearer feedback box
entries.body: Every page outside an article ends with links to Features, Privacy and our contact address. Pointing at the Feedback button shows a card saying what it sends, and the feedback box itself asks for the steps to reproduce a problem, what you expected to see, and what you saw instead.

entries.title: Articles no longer fail while being built
entries.body: Adding an article could fail partway through, leaving its Hierarchy, its Timeline or another panel unbuilt, when the AI wrapped its answer in a sentence or two of its own. The app reads the answer out of the surrounding text instead, and those failures stop.

entries.title: The panel no longer covers the article
entries.body: With the strip that shows your place hidden, some window widths drew the panel over the article text instead of beside it. On phones and the installed app, article text showed through at the top of the screen while a panel was open, and at both edges as the bars slid back. Both are fixed.

entries.title: An address we do not know says so
entries.body: Going to an address the app does not recognise used to show your library, so a mistyped or rotted link looked exactly like a working one. You get a page saying the address was not found, with a link home.

entries.title: The sketch caption moved off the picture
entries.body: In Diagram, a picture's caption appeared as a pop-up wherever your mouse rested on the drawing, covering the parts you were pointing at. It now shows when you point at the Sketch button, or at the title when the picture has only one scene.

entries.title: Adding a PDF survives leaving the page
entries.body: Uploading a PDF continues in the background, so moving to another page part-way through no longer throws away a nearly finished transfer. The Add box takes a link or a file from one button, and the progress page has a working progress bar, a Stop button that really stops the upload, and the same live progress if you reload or open a second tab. An article is never started from a file that did not fully arrive.

entries.title: Paint an illustration without drawing the Sketch first
entries.body: When Illustrated mode has no usable Sketch to paint from — none drawn yet, one that is out of date, or one drawn under a different reading profile — a single button draws the Sketch and then paints. The price and the wait for both steps are shown before you press it, and the message explaining why painting alone was refused no longer contradicts what it goes on to say.

entries.title: Scrolling a long article is smoother
entries.body: Scrolling used to make the page rebuild every paragraph over and over, even when the text had not changed. That work only happens when the text actually changes, so scrolling is smoother, most noticeably on very long articles.

entries.title: Tapping a glossary term keeps its card open
entries.body: On a phone or tablet, tapping an underlined glossary term opened its card and closed it again a fraction of a second later. The card stays open, so you can read the definition, and the button through to the glossary entry is bigger and easier to hit.

entries.title: Clearer reasons when adding an article fails
entries.body: When adding an article fails — a PDF too long, a missing or damaged file, a page with no readable text — the message says what went wrong, and Retry is offered only where trying again can help. A retry keeps the article and the work already paid for, and one interrupted part-way through carries on rather than failing.

entries.title: PDFs of up to 250 pages
entries.body: A PDF of up to 250 pages can now be added, where the limit was 100, and a file over that is turned away before it is stored. Long PDFs come through faster. If one cannot be read because it is password-protected or damaged, the message says which, instead of asking you to try again; and an import that ran out of time no longer says that you stopped it.

entries.title: The reading view scrolls more smoothly
entries.body: Scrolling a long article is smoother than it was, and repeated searches and changes of filter come back sooner. Links to a particular passage also stay pointing at the right place after you have moved around within the article.

entries.title: Your profile shows when a cancelled plan ends
entries.body: If you cancelled your subscription in the billing portal, your profile could still say that the plan renews. It now shows the date your plan ends instead. An account cancelled before this change may still show the old wording, so get in touch if yours does.

entries.title: Plan changes give the right number of articles
entries.body: If you change plan partway through a billing period, the number of articles you can add is adjusted for the part of the period that is left, in the same way the payment is. And if two subscriptions were ever running on one account, you get the larger plan's allowance rather than whichever one started most recently.

entries.title: See whether an article is shared while reading
entries.body: A globe or a padlock sits beside the article title as you read: a globe when the article is shared, a padlock when it is private, and no mark at all when we cannot tell. Click it to go straight to the sharing controls. Until now you had to leave the article to find out, which is rarely where the question comes up. While a change to sharing is being saved the mark goes blank rather than showing you the old state.

entries.title: Sharing controls look like the buttons they are
entries.body: In an article's Access & Sharing panel, the sharing actions had no border or padding, while the labels beside them looked like buttons but did nothing when pressed. The actions are buttons again, each explaining itself when you point at it or reach it with the keyboard, and the labels describe themselves to screen readers.

entries.title: Choose and pay for a plan on Pricing
entries.body: You can pick a plan and pay for it on the Pricing page, rather than going to your profile to buy. Choose one before you sign in and it is still the plan waiting for you when you come back. The plans are described the same way wherever they appear, and when you reach the limit of what your plan allows, the message sends you to the page where you can do something about it.

entries.title: Difficult articles build their levels of detail
entries.body: Some pieces could not be broken into the levels of detail you zoom through, and had to be retried by hand: a very long academic PDF that ended in stray page furniture, an essay whose structure came back inconsistent. Those inconsistencies are now repaired rather than refused, and the levels are built faster than before.

entries.title: Buttons look like buttons
entries.body: Buttons that set no type of their own were drawn in the browser's default typeface, the sign-in button on the front page among them. A few others — the retry on your billing, the two on your settings, Cancel when you write a note — looked like plain text. They now look pressable.

entries.title: Shared articles carry the Timeline and Diagram
entries.body: A shared article now carries the Timeline you already have, and a visitor can open Diagram's Force view without signing in. Neither is listed in the row of modes a signed-out visitor sees, so both open by direct link; the Timeline also appears in a shared article's Metadata.

entries.title: Pricing matches the rest of the site
entries.body: The pricing page now sits in the same layout and navigation as the rest of the site, and the plans appear as cards on Home, Features, Pricing and your profile. Explanatory paragraphs have been replaced by questions and answers, and four statements about billing that did not match what the app actually does have been corrected.

entries.title: Long PDFs finish without you pressing Retry
entries.body: Adding a long or image-heavy PDF could stall or end in an error, leaving you to press Retry. Those documents are now read using less memory, and if the work runs out of time, what has already been built is kept and picked up again rather than started from scratch.

entries.title: PDF section numbers are no longer trimmed
entries.body: When a PDF printed a page number joined to a heading, a digit could be cut from the heading itself, so a section numbered 12.3 showed as 2.3 in the article's outline. A page number is now removed only when the document's numbering predicts it. An article whose outline failed to build once no longer fails every time afterwards.

entries.title: Comments travel with a shared link
entries.body: When you share an article by public link, the comments on it now go too: the passage you marked, what you wrote, and the AI's answer. Referee notes and answers that never finished are left out, and your conversations with the article stay private. The privacy page has been updated to say so.

entries.title: Look up any term in Glossary
entries.body: In an article of your own, Glossary now takes a term you type: it finds the first passage that uses it and explains it there. Nothing is added to the glossary and nothing is kept afterwards. Looking up a term also no longer says it does not appear in the article when it plainly does — the check now searches the whole piece, in any form of the word.

entries.title: Diagram is in the bar for everyone
entries.body: Diagram no longer sits behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page. It is in the bar with the other modes and opens on Sketch; the other kinds of picture stay behind that switch, unless a link you opened asked for one.

entries.title: Illustrated pictures can carry captions
entries.body: Pictures in Illustrated mode can now include short captions on what they draw, repeated in the legend beneath. Illustrating an article is estimated at $0.40 to $0.65, where it was $0.27 to $0.40.

entries.title: PDF limits are shown up front
entries.body: Before you choose a file, the box for adding an article now says a PDF may be up to 50 MB and 250 pages. A long paper used to be refused only after it had uploaded, without saying which limit it had passed.

entries.title: Thirty feedback reports an hour, not ten
entries.body: Feedback used to stop you after ten reports in an hour, which caught people who had just found several things wrong on one page. It is thirty now. The guidance in the box also follows whichever of Problem or Suggestion you picked, rather than one text for both.

entries.title: Footnotes are numbered again, with a way back
entries.body: An article's notes had lost their numbers and any visible way back to the passage that cited them; they are numbered again, in a Notes section of their own, with a return link big enough for a finger. Links out to other sites now open in a new tab, and on a touchscreen the first tap previews one.

entries.title: Sections start at the heading that names them
entries.body: In the levels of detail, a section often began one paragraph after the heading that names it, and the heading was left out; it now opens the section. Articles built before this keep the shape they have until they are built again. When the columns are fitted for you, the most detailed one is dropped first if space runs short.

entries.title: Shared articles show only the Sketch you drew
entries.body: When somebody opens a link you shared and looks at Diagram, they see the Sketch that was drawn for that article, or a line saying nobody has drawn this one yet. A visitor can no longer set a new drawing going. Most articles have never had a Sketch drawn, so that message is what a visitor will usually meet, where before they got a diagram generated on the spot.

entries.title: The Delete button is called Archive
entries.body: Taking an article off your library was labelled Delete, in red, with a bin icon, although the action had always been reversible. It is called Archive now, and says the same thing on your library page, Metadata and Privacy. Archiving a public article takes it out of the public library, but links you have already shared keep working.

entries.title: Column headers sit above the text they name
entries.body: The article is centred in its column, and the header above it and the margin beside it follow it across. The label for the text column no longer sits well to one side of the words it belongs to.

entries.title: The phone keyboard no longer hides the buttons
entries.body: On a phone, opening the keyboard could cover the buttons beneath a text box. They stay in view, the Enter key does what its hint says it will, and nothing is sent while dictation is listening. This applies wherever you type: feedback, comments, chat and notes.

entries.title: Plans stack in price order on a narrow screen
entries.body: On a phone the three plans were listed with the recommended one first, so the prices did not climb as you scrolled. They stack from cheapest to dearest. The recommended plan is still marked by its label, its raised card and its filled button.

entries.title: Ask the AI about a paragraph in place
entries.body: Beside each paragraph of your own articles there is a question mark. Press it and the AI answers about that passage straight away, reopening the conversation you already had about it if there is one. Closing that conversation while the answer is still arriving no longer throws it away; cancelling is a separate button at the foot of it. Pressing the question mark twice no longer buys a second answer.

entries.title: Shared articles appear in a public library
entries.body: Articles you share are listed at /read/public, with their author and where they were published, so someone who was never sent the link can find them. A few of them are shown on the front page and on the features page. If something there is yours and was put up without your permission, the privacy page explains how to ask for it to be taken down.

entries.title: The buttons beside a paragraph are bigger
entries.body: The link, chat and bookmark buttons that appear beside a paragraph sit in a small square block rather than a single column, and each one is large enough to hit reliably with a finger on a tablet. The text sits a little further in to make room for them.

entries.title: Saved searches travel with a shared article
entries.body: Open Search on someone else's public article and you can read the searches they saved: the question, and the passages it matched. You cannot run a new one. Two contradictory messages on an article nobody has searched are gone, and the warning that a search is out of date no longer names causes it cannot know.

entries.title: Long PDFs finish sooner
entries.body: The step that reads the pages of a PDF you add runs many more of them at once, and eases off by itself if the AI service asks it to slow down rather than giving up. Adding a long PDF is faster.

entries.title: Levels of detail no longer repeat themselves
entries.body: When the app works out an article's levels of detail, it leaves out a level that covers exactly the same stretch of text as the one above it. Zooming in gives you something finer at each step instead of the same section twice. This applies to articles added from here on, and to any whose levels are worked out again.

entries.title: Sharing says that the article is listed
entries.body: Turning sharing on used to say only that anyone with the link could read the article. It also lists the article publicly, where someone who was never sent the link can find it, and the wording says so — as does turning sharing off, which takes it off that list. A visitor is told the article was shared publicly.

entries.title: Moving up to a higher plan works
entries.body: Someone already paying for Reader was offered no way to move up to Researcher. The button is there, and the pricing page explains the part-month charge. An account could be sold a second subscription alongside the one it had; it cannot be. The wording shown on a trial no longer promises a part-month credit that a trial does not get.

entries.title: A shared article counts as half an article
entries.body: Making one of your articles public counts it as half an article against your allowance, so sharing leaves you room for more. The count follows what you share: make an article private again and it goes back to costing a full one. The wording around sharing has been corrected too, so it names which of your articles you would actually be charged for, rather than warning about a cost that does not apply to them.

entries.title: Line breaks in code and poetry are kept
entries.body: Text that is laid out in lines - a code sample, a table from a manual, a poem - was flattened into one run of words everywhere except the article itself. That changed what Search matched, the word count shown for an article, and the text every AI-written mode was given. An article now keeps its line breaks wherever it is read.

entries.title: Copy a passage from the comment box
entries.body: Selecting text in an article opens the box where you comment on it, and that box used to take your selection with it, so you had to select the words again to copy them. There is a Copy button beside Close that copies the passage exactly, without saving a comment or closing the box.

entries.title: Controls beside a paragraph sit in a line
entries.body: The marks and controls next to each paragraph are arranged in a single vertical line rather than a square pad, while staying large enough to hit on a touchscreen. The help wording beside them says more plainly what it is for.

entries.title: Notes keep their place when an article updates
entries.body: An article can contain blank lines, rules and empty list items. When one was processed a second time, those places were treated as new every time, which could leave a comment or highlight with nothing to hold on to, and could stop the app finishing the work it does on an article. Both are fixed.

entries.title: An article reopens where you left off
entries.body: Open an article from your library and it comes back as you left it: the same section, the same layout, the same panel beside the article. Chat, Remember and Diagram do not reopen on their own, because each one begins by asking the AI something, though the choices you made inside them are kept. A link someone shared with you still opens exactly where that link points.

entries.title: Dictation drops the ums and ahs
entries.body: When you dictate, common filler words are deleted from what gets written down, from a fixed list, so nothing you said is rephrased. The microphone will not start while you are offline, and a failed transcription keeps your recording and offers Try again rather than losing it.

entries.title: A contact page, and a tidier Feedback box
entries.body: There is a Contact link in the footer, with an address you can write to. The Feedback box thanks you for what you sent, shuts without blanking the form first, and keeps anything typed after you press Send as the start of your next note. A screenshot still being prepared can no longer end up on the wrong report.

entries.title: PDFs get the article's own title and author
entries.body: A PDF was sometimes added to your library under the journal's name rather than the paper's, because a front page's masthead and submission dates look much like a title. Those are told apart from the title now, and a PDF is given its author for the first time, which Referee mode uses to tell a paper's authors apart.

entries.title: Questions about a passage get a teaching answer
entries.body: When you ask a question about a paragraph, the answer is written to help you work the passage out rather than hand you a conclusion. Follow-up questions in a conversation attached to a passage now always arrive with that passage, so the answer stays about the text in front of you, and the AI will search the web when a question needs evidence from outside the article.

entries.title: Summary entries come with a question
entries.body: The top-level entries in Summary mode now show a question about the section rather than a one-line description of it — something to try answering for yourself before you read on. Questions are kept when you open a section up into more detail, and a question that only restated the description is left out.

entries.title: Pictures can fill the screen in Illustrated
entries.body: On a wide display, Illustrated mode can give the picture a full-height column of its own that scrolls separately from the text. You can read what the piece says about a picture while the picture stays in view.

entries.title: Switching modes is quicker on long articles
entries.body: Moving between modes on a very long article was slow enough to notice. Switching to Hierarchy now takes 39% less time than it did, Summary 33% less and Outline 63% less, and the page has more room to respond while it happens.

entries.title: More room for the text beside each paragraph
entries.body: The controls beside each paragraph — mark, link, chat and ask — now collapse into a single dot on short paragraphs and appear in full on wider ones; press the dot to unfold them. Short paragraphs no longer stretch to fit them, and the narrower column gives the text 24 pixels back on each side.

entries.title: Tidier Glossary and Quotes panels
entries.body: The Glossary panel has lost its Start again button, which threw away everything the panel had found, and the line of build details beneath it. That line is gone from the Quotes panel and the bar above the article too. Find more now shows progress the moment you press it, so you cannot start a second run by mistake.

entries.title: A note about reading on a small screen
entries.body: On a narrow touch screen there is room for the article or one of the modes, but not both, so opening a mode covers the article. A short banner now says that this is deliberate, suggests turning the screen sideways, and stays dismissed on that device once you close it.

entries.title: The conversation count reopens your conversation
